When material is removed during machining, the equilibrium between compressive and tensile stress can cause the part to warp and deform, resulting in loss of geometric part accuracy. During fabrication of brazed NCRF structures, some workpieces will undergo a stress-relieving heat treatment at 500oC. While beneficial for geometric accuracy, this stress- relieve process will soften the hardened copper, losing any high gradient advantages. In the following, we assume this issue has already been address via strict source of feedstock material as well as detailed machining strategies developed by the National Labs working in conjunction with industry. Notably X-band CLIC structures required a flatness of <1 μm, roughness of R <25 nm and form accuracy of ±2.5 μm. Turning has the distinct advantage that the cutting surface has a a singular, well defined edge and the cutting tool itself is stationary, thereby limiting vibrations. From a design perspective, turning has a distinct disadvantage in that the geometry being turned should be rotationally symmetric. Advanced machine tool configurations are possible, including synchronized tool/chuck motion as well as the use of ‘mill-turn’ type lathes, which combines both milling and turning within a single machine but stop start motion and tool engagement / disengagement must be controlled carefully in order to not spoil the pristine surfaces. During the fabrication of the SwissFEL linacs, PSI developed a lathe-based turning process in-house before transferring technology to industry for series production [14]. The primary requirements were a environmentally-controlled machining facility (18.50°C +/- 0.1°C, <50% relative humidity), pneumatically stabilized slanted bed lathe and poly and mono-crystalline diamond (PCD, MCD) cutting tools. The result was a form tolerances of ± 2 μm with a surface finish Ra <25 nm and concentricity of less than 50 μm on the disk structures [15]. When combined with the automated robotic assembly, the SwissFEL linac did not require any post braze tuning. Compared to turning, milling involves a rotating cutting tool with multiple cutting surfaces and a quasi- stationary workpiece. The lever arm of the rotating cutting tool, as well as asymmetry in the cutting tool surfaces can lead to issues regarding form and finish accuracy. But unlike turning, milling enables the formation of complex and precise shapes with a single part setup especially when 5-axis machining technology is employed. Milling and turning are complementary technologies which can often be used in conjunction, as shown in the ELI-NP cell design demonstrated by INFN.
